props.title: A Time for Drunken Horses

sections.content: A Time for Drunken Horses (2000) marks a pivotal moment in Iranian Kurdish cinema, delivering a raw portrayal of survival along the Iran-Iraq border. Director Bahman Ghobadi's debut feature throws us into the harsh reality of Kurdish children forced into smuggling to survive, echoing the unflinching child-centered narratives of Children of Heaven (1997) and The Apple (1998). The film's title refers to the smugglers giving alcohol to their horses to help them endure freezing mountain passages - a brutal metaphor for the desperate measures required for survival.

sections.content: Ghobadi's documentary-like approach aligns with other Iranian New Wave masterworks, but pushes further into previously unexplored Kurdish territory. Like The Wind Will Carry Us (1999) and Taste of Cherry (1997), the film employs non-professional actors and natural settings to devastating effect. The story of young Ayoub's struggle to pay for his disabled brother's surgery while caring for his siblings creates an intimate portrait of Kurdish resilience that transcends political boundaries.

The film's influence resonates through later works examining children in conflict zones, from Osama (2003) to Beasts of No Nation (2015). Its unflinching gaze at child labor and border economies exposed realities rarely seen in cinema before, while maintaining the poetic visual style characteristic of Iranian art house films of the period. sections.content: A Time for Drunken Horses helped establish Kurdish cinema's distinct voice in world film. Its success paved the way for works like My Sweet Pepper Land (2013) and Songs of My Homeland (2014), which further explored Kurdish identity and struggle. The film's focus on children's resilience in extreme circumstances connects to a broader tradition of Middle Eastern cinema, from Where is the Friend's Home? (1987) to Capernaum (2018), while maintaining its uniquely Kurdish perspective.
